evaluation.positioning_hook: A burned-out ex-soldier with a hidden drinking problem takes a security job for a Glasgow crime boss, then starts sniffing out the betrayal that nearly got him killed.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clean commercial lane: a hard-edged crime story with a damaged ex-military lead, a gangland power structure, and a strong antihero voice. The appeal is strongest for adult thriller audiences and buyers who like character-first genre pieces rather than broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening assassination attempt, the five-year jump, and the recruitment by Roddy Kincaid establish the engine quickly and clearly. The premise is easy to explain, though the script is more about character and atmosphere than a single high-concept twist.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Knox is built as a watchable contradiction: disciplined, sarcastic, physically capable, and visibly trying to keep himself together. Kincaid has enough swagger and menace to carry scenes, while the supporting players give the world texture, even if the script is still centered heavily on the Knox/Kincaid dynamic.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The material leans on familiar crime-thriller architecture, but it gives it a distinct Scottish voice, recovery-room irony, and a lead who is as much self-management as action. The boldest choice is the tonal blend of bruising violence with dry, almost stand-up-level banter.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening attack, the time jump, and the recruitment sequence keep the pages moving, and the dialogue has snap. The script is strongest as a set of escalating encounters; the forward drive is clear, though the feature shape here still reads more like a launchpad than a fully escalated endgame.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The ex-soldier-in-gangland setup is familiar, but the specific voice, the Scottish milieu, and the recovery framing give it a recognizable identity. It feels like a version of the genre that knows its own local rhythms rather than a generic import.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The gym, the nightclub office, the AA meeting, the church confessional, and the hotel security world all suggest a lived-in ecosystem with its own codes. The script understands how money, loyalty, addiction, and image circulate through that environment.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is sharply identifiable: violent but jokey, profane but emotionally bruised, streetwise without losing the recovery undercurrent. The script’s voice is one of its most marketable assets because the banter and menace feel inseparable.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are clear seeds of deeper material in Knox’s sobriety, his military past, and the priest/confessional exchange with Kincaid. The draft hints at a larger moral and psychological story beneath the crime plot, though this excerpt keeps that depth mostly in suggestion.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Knox and Kincaid are a strong central pairing, and Craig/Darren/Sloane/Rab add useful friction around them. The ensemble is functional and playable, though the script still lives most powerfully in the lead relationship and the orbit around it.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming crime thriller / premium cable feature lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to festival-to-platform, streamer original, or limited theatrical crime title.

cost.note: Contemporary settings, modest cast, and no VFX-heavy set pieces keep the budget in a contained feature range.

cast.note: The lead roles depend on strong, specific performers with Scottish dialect comfort, plus a child flashback role and a playable supporting ensemble.

location.note: The story moves through several distinct interiors and night exteriors, but all are grounded, practical locations rather than large-scale builds.

content.note: Violence, threats, profanity, and addiction material place it firmly in mature territory without pushing into extreme content.

rights.note: No named real people, brands, music cues, or IP-dependent elements are featured prominently.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a lead role actors can really sink into: a man who is physically capable, verbally sharp, and visibly trying to keep his life from sliding back into chaos. Mid-budget crime buyers and prestige-minded casting directors will see a part that can anchor the whole film on performance alone.
strengths.evidence: The opening bathroom ritual, the AA meeting, and the later reveal of his sobriety and PTSD all frame him as controlled on the surface and unstable underneath.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dialogue has a lived-in Scottish bite.
strengths.what_it_means: That voice gives the script a commercial identity that separates it from generic gangland material and makes the read feel local, specific, and castable. Directors and buyers looking for regional crime with personality will respond to the rhythm, slang, and comic aggression.
strengths.evidence: The AA meeting, the gym banter, and Knox’s exchanges with Kincaid all carry a distinct vernacular and comic timing.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Knox/Kincaid dynamic is instantly playable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a central two-hander engine that can carry the movie even before the larger conspiracy fully opens up. Actors who like sparring, status games, and shifting alliances will see a showcase in the way the two men test each other from the confessional to the nightclub office.
strengths.evidence: Kincaid hires Knox after the alleyway rescue, then immediately probes his background and loyalty in the office scene.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels operational, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: The gym, the nightclub, the church, the hotel security detail, and the betting scheme all create a usable ecosystem for a producer — each space generates story, leverage, and status. Buyers who like contained crime worlds with clear hierarchy will see a film that can be made efficiently while still feeling populated.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from AA to gym to office to boxing venue to confessional to alleyway without losing the sense of one connected underworld.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Recovery is woven into the crime story.
strengths.what_it_means: That adds a second emotional lane beyond the gangland plot, which broadens the audience beyond pure genre fans and gives the film a more adult, reflective aftertaste. Actors and directors drawn to damaged-men material will see a role and a world that can hold both menace and vulnerability.
strengths.evidence: The AA meeting, the church confessional, the flask, and Knox’s repeated insistence that he is clean all sit inside the same narrative frame.

whats_special.headline: This is a sharp, actor-friendly crime feature with a real voice: a Scottish ex-soldier trying to stay sober gets pulled into a gangland security job and immediately starts reading the room for betrayal. The hook is not just the plot mechanics — it’s the combination of bruised masculinity, dry humor, and a lived-in underworld that makes the material feel castable and saleable.

lead_characters.name: Jack Knox
lead_characters.hook: Knox is a hard-edged, hyper-observant man who performs control even when he’s barely holding himself together. He’s sober, funny in a cutting way, and physically capable, but the script keeps revealing the cost of that competence through the flask, the AA meeting, the PTSD admission, and the way he reads danger before anyone else does.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Matthew McConaughey in True Detective season 1 — a damaged, magnetic man whose intelligence and self-mythology are part of the performance. It gives an actor the chance to play menace, wit, vulnerability, and tactical intelligence in one role, with enough internal contradiction to carry a whole feature.

lead_characters.name: Roddy Kincaid
lead_characters.demographics: Male · 40s-50s · Scottish · crime boss / nightclub operator
lead_characters.hook: Kincaid is a polished predator: charming, profane, suspicious, and always testing the room for leverage. He can talk like a confessor, threaten like a gangster, and pivot into business mode in the same breath, which makes him feel like a man who survives by reading people faster than they read him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Tom Hardy in Legend or Brian Cox in Succession — a charismatic authority figure whose volatility is always one sentence away from surfacing. It gives an actor the chance to play command, paranoia, and dark comedy without ever leaving the scene.

lead_characters.name: Craig
lead_characters.hook: Craig is the blunt instrument in Kincaid’s orbit, all attitude, bruised ego, and physical presence. He’s the kind of supporting player who instantly creates friction because he thinks in threats, not strategy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that plays like Walton Goggins in Justified — a side character with enough swagger, resentment, and comic bite to steal scenes. Character actors who specialize in volatile henchmen and scene-stealing pressure-cookers will want it.

lead_characters.name: Darren
lead_characters.hook: Darren is Craig’s sharper, more verbally agile counterpart, still dangerous but more likely to needle than simply charge. He gives the world a second flavor of menace and helps make Kincaid’s operation feel like a real hierarchy rather than a one-note crew.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting part that has the rhythm of Michael K. Williams in The Wire — a street-level operator with enough personality to register immediately. Actors who like playing intelligence inside criminal muscle will see a clean, playable lane.

lead_characters.name: Sloane Kincaid
lead_characters.hook: Sloane is the one person in the room who can look at Knox without being impressed by his performance. She’s sharp, skeptical, and business-minded, which gives the Kincaid world a younger, more controlled counterweight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the grounded authority of Sarah Snook in Succession — someone who can hold a room with a look and a line. It offers dry intelligence, family tension, and the chance to play competence inside a criminal family structure.

lead_characters.name: Rab
lead_characters.hook: Rab is a worn-down local operator whose pride is outrunning his finances. He’s the human cost of the world Knox is stepping into, and his desperation gives the gym storyline emotional stakes beyond the betting scheme.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that gives an actor the grounded pathos of Stephen Graham in smaller-scale crime drama work — a man whose face tells the story before the dialogue does. Character actors who can play debt, shame, and loyalty in one scene will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Maureen
lead_characters.hook: Maureen is a comic pressure valve with a tragic edge, the kind of AA-room presence who can turn a meeting into a whole worldview. Her monologue is funny, chaotic, and painfully specific, which makes her feel lived-in rather than written as a gag.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Brenda Blethyn in a kitchen-sink drama — a role that can pivot from comedy to pathos in a single breath. A veteran character actress would relish the chance to land a scene that is both hilarious and bruised.

lead_characters.name: Kieran
lead_characters.hook: Kieran is a small but vivid presence in the boxing gym, a kid who gives Knox a glimpse of gentleness inside a violent world. He helps humanize Knox without sentimentalizing him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a brief but memorable child role in the tradition of the kid scenes in The Wrestler — the kind of part that gives a young performer a clear emotional beat opposite an adult lead. It’s a clean showcase for naturalism and timing.

lead_characters.name: Patrick - Priest
lead_characters.hook: The priest is dry, unsentimental, and more streetwise than pious, which makes the confessional scene feel like a negotiation rather than a sermon. He’s there to puncture Roddy’s self-justifications and keep the moral pressure alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that has the verbal authority of Mark Rylance in a dialogue scene — calm, precise, and quietly dominant. Character actors who enjoy sparring with a gangster while sounding spiritually unflappable will want it.

lead_characters.name: Barbara
lead_characters.hook: Barbara is a transactional, seductive presence who enters the story with immediate mystery and then flips the room’s power balance. She’s less a romantic interest than a tactical move in Kincaid’s world, which makes her feel dangerous in a different register.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable femme-fatale-adjacent role that gives an actress the cool control of Rebecca Ferguson in a scene like this — a woman who can change the temperature of a room without overexplaining herself. It’s a clean showcase for allure, timing, and subtext.

lead_characters.name: Alex
lead_characters.hook: Alex is a small but useful texture piece in the recovery circle, a man whose one-line introduction widens the social world around Knox. He helps make the meeting feel populated by actual lives rather than exposition delivery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small role that character actors use to make a room feel real, similar to the AA-circle texture in Flight or The Fighter. It gives an actor a quick, specific beat in a scene that already has strong ensemble energy.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a crime film where the jokes land as hard as the punches.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two features, or TV directors moving into features, who already work comfortably with performance-forward crime material and regional specificity. This rewards directors who like contained worlds, sharp dialogue, and scenes that turn on status, not spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The material gives a director a chance to stage tension through behavior, timing, and reversals rather than big set pieces, which is exactly the kind of craft lane that can elevate a modestly budgeted feature. It will attract filmmakers who want to prove they can handle genre while keeping the camera close to actors and the tone precise.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streamer crime lane / festival-friendly adult thriller
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be packaged around two strong lead performances without requiring VFX or large-scale action, which makes it viable for a director-led greenlight or a castable indie package. The Scottish crime voice and mature addiction angle give it exportable genre appeal with enough specificity to stand out in a crowded adult-thriller market.

considerations.area: The opening attack is doing a lot at once.
considerations.detail: The hotel-bathroom-to-car-park sequence is vivid and efficient, but the version of the opening where Knox’s competence is seeded a beat earlier could make the betrayal hit even harder. One primary lever would be to clarify the relationship between Knox, McKissack, and Siddiqui before the ambush so the audience feels the loss as well as the shock.

considerations.area: The feature shape is still mostly launch energy.
considerations.detail: The excerpt builds a strong setup, recruitment, and alliance-testing run, and the next pass can focus on the larger escalation that turns this from a compelling premise into a full feature engine. A producer will want to see the endgame pressure point as clearly as the opening hook.

considerations.area: The supporting crew could carry more independent motion.
considerations.detail: Craig, Darren, Sloane, and Rab all register cleanly, and the version of the script where one or two of them have a more distinct agenda would widen the ensemble’s story-generating power. That would also give the film more playable scenes outside the Knox/Kincaid axis.

The alleyway, street, car park, and boxing-venue exterior work all cluster into a practical but shoot-heavy block of material. A simplification pass that keeps the same pressure but folds one exterior beat into another would protect the pace and make the schedule easier to manage.
